prompt: a close-up photo of bare mirror-like polished aluminium metal, unpainted and highly reflective
notes: Polished aluminum; highly reflective, very low emissivity. BARE metal only - painted aluminium is painted_metal. Solar absorptance also low: bright bare metal reflects most shortwave.

prompt: a close-up photo of bare dull oxidized aluminium metal, unpainted
notes: Heavily oxidized aluminum. BARE metal only. Dull/oxidized finish roughly doubles solar absorptance vs. polished.

prompt: a close-up photo of bare dark oxidized steel metal, unpainted
notes: Oxidized steel. BARE metal only. Dark oxide layer absorbs shortwave almost as strongly as it emits longwave.

prompt: a photo of a painted metal radiator or painted metal panel with glossy enamel paint
notes: Painted/enamelled metal (radiators, painted panels, painted pipes). Paint dominates the surface, so emissivity is that of paint, NOT of the metal underneath. Solar absorptance is strongly color-dependent (0.3 light/0.95 dark) -- 0.65 is a mid-tone placeholder, override per-voxel if paint color is known.

notes: Glass (non-transparent to LWIR). Solar absorptance low because clear glass mostly transmits/reflects shortwave rather than absorbing it -- most solar gain through glass is transmission, not captured by an opaque-surface absorptance model.

prompt: a photo of a black rubber surface
notes: Rubber, hard or soft. Solar absorptance stays high even for lighter tints (blue-grey, etc): NIR-absorbing carbon-filled compounds in the rubber, not surface pigment, dominate shortwave absorption -- unlike paint, color is a weak predictor here. 0.80 (session 9 corridor: medium blue-grey hard rubber flooring, see photo) is the low end of the class range, not a light-surface value like paint/plaster would get for the same visible tone.
